summary: Across 30 simulated cells (400 paired trials each), inverse-variance weighting generally brought empirical Wald-interval coverage closer to 95% than OLS, but both methods undercovered. The hypothesized reduction in estimator spread was not observed: weighted estimates were typically slightly more variable than OLS. Increasing the number of time points strongly reduced spread, while all nonlinear fits passed numerical checks.
key_findings: All cells were numerically successful: 0 of 400 planned trials failed in each reported cell (Wilson 95% upper bound 0.0095). The pre-run Arrhenius recovery, rate-ratio, centering, delta-method, and centroid oracles all passed.

[by_Arrhenius_regression_method] At 0.25% noise and 5 time points, Ea coverage was identical for OLS and weighted fitting: 0.870 (348/400; Wilson 95% CI 0.833–0.899). Thus weighting did not improve calibration uniformly.

[by_Arrhenius_regression_method] In visible higher-information cells, weighted Ea coverage was closer to nominal than OLS but still below 0.95: at 8% noise and 20 points, 0.915 (366/400; 0.884–0.939) versus 0.813 (325/400; 0.771–0.848); at 8% noise and 32 points, 0.918 (367/400; 0.886–0.941) versus 0.870 (348/400; 0.833–0.899). ln A coverage followed the same pattern (0.923 versus 0.820 at 8% noise and 20 points).

[by_n_time_points] Estimate spread declined sharply with additional time points. At 8% noise, weighted Ea SD fell from 2,030 J mol^-1 at 5 points to 717 J mol^-1 at 32 points; weighted ln A SD fell from 0.771 to 0.276. The corresponding OLS decreases were 1,920 to 709 J mol^-1 and 0.745 to 0.272.

[by_Arrhenius_regression_method] Weighting did not reduce spread in the reported cells. For example, at 8% noise and 20 points, weighted versus OLS Ea SD was 923 versus 909 J mol^-1, and at 8% noise and 32 points it was 717 versus 709 J mol^-1. At 0.25% noise and 5 points, it was 64.0 versus 56.5 J mol^-1.

[by_Arrhenius_regression_method] Ea and ln A estimates were extremely positively correlated in every displayed cell (approximately 0.995–0.997), consistent with strong slope–intercept coupling when recovering the uncentered Arrhenius intercept.

Bias was small relative to the true Ea of 24,122 J mol^-1: the largest displayed weighted Ea mean bias was 154 J mol^-1 (about 0.64%), meeting the pre-specified 5% absolute-bias criterion, although some bootstrap bias intervals exclude zero.

claims_supported.evidence: At 8% noise, weighted Ea SD declined from 2,030 J mol^-1 (5 points) to 717 J mol^-1 (32 points), with the analogous OLS decline from 1,920 to 709 J mol^-1.

claims_supported.claim: The nominal-Wald intervals are undercalibrated under this two-stage procedure.
claims_supported.evidence: Observed Ea coverage ranged from 0.813 to 0.918 in the displayed cells, and even weighted coverage intervals remained below the nominal 0.95 target (for example, 0.884–0.939 at 8% noise and 20 points).

claims_supported.claim: Weighting is associated with better observed interval coverage in many non-minimal time-point cells.
claims_supported.evidence: At 8% noise, weighted Ea coverage was 0.905–0.918 across 8–32 points, versus OLS 0.813–0.878; however, formal paired coverage contrasts were not supplied.

claims_supported.claim: The kinetic fitting procedure was numerically reliable on this simulation grid.
claims_supported.evidence: All reported cells had 400 successful trials and zero failures; all specified pre-run numerical and analytical oracles passed.

claims_unsupported.claim: Inverse-variance weighting reduces Ea or ln A estimator spread relative to OLS.
claims_unsupported.reason: Displayed weighted SDs are generally slightly larger than their OLS counterparts.
Weighted coverage estimates were below 0.95 throughout the displayed results, with Wilson intervals also below 0.95 in the cited cells.

claims_unsupported.claim: Weighting improves coverage in every grid cell.
claims_unsupported.reason: At 0.25% noise and 5 points, both methods had identical 0.870 Ea and ln A coverage.

claims_unsupported.claim: Method differences are statistically significant after multiplicity control.
claims_unsupported.reason: The supplied comparison-statistics block contains no estimable contrasts, effect sizes, p-values, or Holm-adjusted results.

limitations: Only one simulation seed was run; there is no between-seed replication interval.
Coverage uncertainty is binomial and cell-specific: Wilson intervals are often wider than ±0.025, so the intended coverage precision was not attained for many cells.

Formal paired method-comparison statistics were unavailable because the comparison engine marked the requested metrics unsupported; observed method differences should not be presented as significance-tested.

The simulation uses five exact temperatures, first-order kinetics, independently scaled sampling windows, and additive independent concentration noise; conclusions do not establish performance under correlated, proportional, or model-misspecified errors.
The run took 111.3 seconds, exceeding the stated under-60-second compute target.
